summary:
On 22 April 2024 the High Court of Justice in Roseau held that sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act were unconstitutional insofar as they criminalised consensual same-sex activity between adults. Reporting on 23 and 24 April 2024 recorded the outcome as decriminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct between adults in Dominica, in a case brought by a gay man living in Dominica.

The court ordered a reading-down rather than a full repeal. Section 14(2) is to be read as exempting private consensual sexual acts between adult persons who consent, and section 16(1)(b) is to be read as exempting private consensual adult acts from the 10-year penalty for buggery.

The prior regime was broad. It criminalised male same-sex sexual activity and female same-sex sexual activity, as well as anal intercourse between persons of the opposite sex. Under the Sexual Offences Act 1998 as amended in 2016, section 14 on gross indecency provided 12 years imprisonment where the complainant was 16 or older, and 14 years for a first offence and 20 years for a subsequent offence where the complainant was under 16, with an exemption only for private consensual adult male-female acts. Section 16 on buggery provided 25 years where committed by an adult on a minor, 10 years where committed by an adult on another adult, 5 years where committed by a minor, and 4 years for attempt or assault with intent to commit buggery, with judicial discretion to order admission to a psychiatric hospital for treatment.

Enforcement before the ruling included custodial and medical penalties. Between 1995 and 2000 there were 35 arrests for buggery resulting in fines and prison sentences of up to 10 years, with some persons sent to psychiatric hospitals for treatment. In 2001, 15 women were sentenced to five years imprisonment for gross indecency and 10 men were sentenced to five years for engaging in gross indecency with persons of the same sex. In 2014 the Prime Minister stated that Dominica did not enforce the law against homosexual activity at least in private homes and had no plans to do so.

Dominica provides no recognition to same-sex unions as marriage or civil unions. No law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Protection gaps are documented in police response. The gay man who filed suit in July 2019 challenging the 10-year and 12-year provisions reported that police refused to investigate a vicious home attack and reported physical and sexual assaults because gay people were considered criminals under Dominican law. More generally, reports to police by victims are reported as not taken seriously, with victims sometimes ridiculed.

Violence and intimidation linked to perceived sexual orientation are reported. Sources describe suspected hate crimes against individuals believed to be homosexuals, vandalism against property of openly gay persons, and use in disputes of derogatory terms such as buggerman or battyman to refer to effeminate men. As an example of lethal violence within that pattern, Clement James of Portsmouth was stabbed to death in 2010 after being accused of watching his male assailant in a public place. The accused, Davis St Jean, was reported to preach in the street about killing gay people and to have said all battie boi must dead before the stabbing.

Hostility toward gay visitors has been expressed publicly. In 2009 the president of the Evangelical Association, Bill Daniel, stated that the government should ensure gay tourists do not come to the island and conduct themselves in any immoral way, in a context of association protests against gay cruises visiting the island and against promotion of Dominica as a gay tourist destination.
tangentialFactors:
An international human rights dispatch on 24 April 2024 that reported the High Court decision called for all Caribbean nations to repeal comparable criminal laws.

Activists hailed the ruling as a significant milestone in the ongoing struggle for LGBTQ rights in the Caribbean.

In 2013 Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire of Dominica publicly called for eliminating criminal penalties for homosexuality and for ending all forms of violence against LGBT people, citing the position of the Holy See.

On 22 March 2011 Dominica was listed among 85 signatories to a joint statement in the Human Rights Council on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The signature stands as a dated diplomatic commitment on the record.
localsOnly:
Minority Rights Dominica, known as MiRiDom and founded by Darryl Philip, operates as an LGBTQ advocacy group in Dominica.

The provisions later struck down had been under constitutional challenge for years. On 20 July 2019 Dominica News Online reported that MiRiDom founder Daryl Phillip had announced at a news conference that a High Court challenge to the buggery and sexual-activity provisions had been filed.

A 2011 academic submission to the United Nations stated that LGBTQ groups were forced to operate underground for fear members would be victimised.
outOfScopeNotes:
Not sourced in the inventory are rules that would specifically determine a trans visitor's administrative experience, including gender-marker rules for identity documents, entry and visa treatment, airport or border screening practice, access to sex-segregated facilities, and access to gender-affirming care. No finding on those points can be stated from the sources provided.

No documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically is provided in the sources. The extent of trans-specific risk as distinct from risk linked to same-sex conduct is therefore unresolved.

One listed source is a United States State Department press statement relating to Dominica for which no usable substantive content was supplied. It supports no finding.
